title: English Vocabulary 1 · Units 27–28
description: Units 27–28 reviewed against the illustrated teaching pages, exercises and British-English phonemic index, with original examples and English-language usage notes.
sourceNotice: Lexical and pedagogical targets follow the user-supplied published reference material. All explanations and example sentences are original; published exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 27: the illustrated continent/country table, nationality endings, capitals, languages and exercises 27.1–27.5, including the independent geography follow-up. Unit 28: illustrated weather phenomena, noun/adjective patterns, weather expressions, warnings, forecast tip and exercises 28.1–28.5.
audit.pronunciation: British-English IPA compared with the textbook phonemic index (PDF pages 160–170) for indexed headwords; unindexed geographical names and multiword expressions were reviewed compositionally but not independently certified by a pronunciation dictionary.
audit.cannotGuarantee: Static syntax and content validation do not establish browser import, TTS quality, listening/pronunciation practice, adaptive progress continuity, or backup/restore compatibility. Human editorial approval remains outstanding.

editorialReview.reviewMethod: Direct inspection of four illustrated textbook pages, tables, questions and exercise graphics, review of each original target and IPA cross-check against the book index where present. Existing target IDs preserved.
editorialReview.notes: The original package, unit and item IDs were retained. Additional exercise-linked targets have new unique IDs. Real application playback and progress-restoration were not tested.

units.title: Unit 27 — Countries and nationalities
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 27. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.note: A continent is a large land area. The names of continents begin with capital letters.

items.example: Italy is a country in Europe.
items.note: The plural is countries. Country names always begin with capital letters.
North America is a continent; Canada and the USA are countries in it.
South America is a continent; Brazil and Peru are examples of countries in it.
Europe is a continent; the first letter is capitalised.
Africa is a continent. Do not write africa with a lower-case first letter.
Asia is a continent. The first letter of the name is capitalised.
The textbook uses Australia both for the country and as the name of a continent in its simplified table.
Antarctica is a continent, not the name of a country. Keep the capital letter.

items.example: Canada is north of the USA.
items.note: The nationality adjective is Canadian. Canada appears in the North America column.

items.example: My friend lives in the USA.
items.note: The is normally used before USA, short for the United States of America. The US is another form.
The US means the United States. US is pronounced as the two letter names, not the word us.
The nationality adjective in the book is Argentinian, with an -ian ending.
The nationality adjective is Brazilian. The final letter of Brazil is l.
Chile is in South America. Chilean is a useful additional nationality adjective not listed in the source nationality table.
The country is spelt Colombia, not Columbia. The nationality adjective is Colombian.
Peru is in South America; the nationality adjective is Peruvian.

items.example: Cairo is the capital of Egypt.
items.note: Egypt is in Africa. Egyptian is the corresponding nationality adjective.
Morocco is in Africa. The nationality adjective is Moroccan.

items.example: South Africa is a country in Africa.
items.note: South Africa is a country in the continent of Africa; do not confuse the two names.
Tunisia is a country in Africa; the corresponding nationality adjective is Tunisian.
Germany is in Europe. German describes nationality and also names the language.

items.example: Rome is the capital of Italy.
items.note: Italy is in Europe. Its nationality adjective is Italian.
Poland is a country in Europe. The corresponding nationality is Polish.
Spain is a country in Europe; Spanish can describe nationality and the language.

items.example: London is the capital of the UK.
items.note: The UK stands for the United Kingdom and normally takes the definite article the.
New Zealand is a country in the book’s Australia continent column. A person from there is a New Zealander.
China is a country in Asia; Chinese is the nationality adjective and a language name.
India is a country in Asia; Indian is the nationality adjective.

items.example: Tokyo is the capital of Japan.
items.note: Japan is a country in Asia; Japanese is the nationality adjective and language name.
Pakistan is in Asia. The book lists Pakistani as an exceptional nationality ending.
Thailand is in Asia; Thai is the nationality adjective and language name.
American is a nationality adjective; capitalise the A. The context here is the USA.
Argentinian is the nationality adjective used in the textbook; Argentine is another common alternative.
Australian is the nationality adjective for Australia and ends in -ian.
Brazilian is the nationality adjective for Brazil; capitalise the B.
Canadian is the nationality adjective for Canada and ends in -ian.
Colombian is the nationality adjective from Colombia, spelt with o, not u.
Egyptian ends in -ian in spelling, but the final syllable is pronounced /ʃən/.
German is a nationality adjective and also a language name. It is always capitalised.
Indian is the nationality adjective for India and ends in -ian.
Italian describes nationality or the language; it begins with a capital letter.
Moroccan is the nationality adjective for Morocco. Notice its -an ending.
Peruvian is the nationality adjective for Peru; do not form it by simply adding -ian.
South African is a two-word nationality adjective; capitalise both words.
Tunisian is the nationality adjective for Tunisia; its suffix is -ian.
British refers to Britain and is not exactly the same as English, which refers to England.
English describes England or the English language. The first letter is always capitalised.
Finnish is a nationality and language adjective with an -ish ending. Finland is not listed in the country table.
Irish describes Ireland or its people and ends in -ish.
Polish, with a capital P, is a nationality adjective and language name. Lower-case polish is a different English word.
Scottish refers to Scotland and ends in -ish; Scottish is not synonymous with English.
Spanish describes a nationality and is also the name of the language. Capitalise S.
Chinese can describe nationality and the language. The final syllable has long /iː/.
Japanese is an adjective or language name, with the final stressed /iːz/ sound.
Portuguese is the nationality adjective and the language name. It ends in -ese.
Pakistani has the exceptional nationality ending -i, rather than the more frequent -ian.
Thai is both a nationality adjective and a language name; it does not follow the -ian/-ish/-ese patterns.
French describes nationality and the language. It is listed as an exception to the regular suffix patterns.

items.example: We listened to a song in Arabic.
items.note: Arabic is a language name. The book notes that a language name need not match the corresponding nationality adjective.

items.example: Rome is a capital city in Europe.
items.note: A capital city is the main administrative city of a country; the exercise practises the capital of + country.

items.example: Tokyo is the capital of Japan.
items.note: Tokyo is the capital of Japan; both names begin with capital letters.

items.example: Rome is the capital of Italy.
items.note: Rome is the capital of Italy. Say the capital of Italy, not the Italy capital.

items.example: Canberra is the capital of Australia.
items.note: Canberra, not Sydney, is the capital of Australia.

items.example: Bogotá is the capital of Colombia.
items.note: Bogotá is the capital of Colombia. English pronunciation and spelling with or without the accent may vary.

items.example: Cairo is the capital of Egypt.
items.note: Cairo is the capital of Egypt; the English pronunciation begins /kaɪ/.

items.example: London is the capital of the UK.
items.note: London is the capital of the UK. Use the before UK.

items.example: Berlin is the capital of Germany.
items.note: Berlin is the capital of Germany; stress the final syllable in the usual English pronunciation.

items.example: Warsaw is the capital of Poland.
items.note: Warsaw is the capital of Poland; it has two syllables in English.

items.example: Buenos Aires is the capital of Argentina.
items.note: Buenos Aires is the capital of Argentina. British English pronunciation varies.

items.example: Madrid is the capital of Spain.
items.note: Madrid is the capital of Spain; stress the second syllable in standard British English.

items.example: I can speak more than one language.
items.note: Use speak + a language: speak English, speak Spanish. This pattern extends the language exercise.
Icelandic is the name of the language used in the model answer for exercise 27.3.

items.example: England is part of the UK.
items.note: England is mentioned in the exercise on languages; the related adjective is English.

items.example: Iceland is an island country in the North Atlantic.
items.note: Iceland is contrasted with English-speaking countries in exercise 27.3; its language is Icelandic.

items.example: Spanish is widely spoken in Mexico.
items.note: Mexico appears in the exercise on languages, alongside Spain and other countries.
Do not confuse Austria with Australia. Austria appears in the exercise about languages.

items.example: Several languages are spoken in Switzerland.
items.note: Switzerland appears in language comparisons; it has several national languages, including German, French and Italian.

items.example: Arabic is spoken in Saudi Arabia.
items.note: Saudi Arabia is used in the exercise on Arabic-speaking countries.
France is mentioned in the exercise on languages; the corresponding language is French.

items.example: Scotland is part of the UK.
items.note: Scotland appears in exercise 27.3; Scottish is the corresponding nationality adjective.

items.example: Canberra is the capital of Australia.
items.note: Use the capital of + country. This structure is required in exercise 27.2.

items.example: Many people in Canada speak English.
items.note: Say speak English, not speak in English, to name the language someone knows.

items.example: Many people in Morocco speak Arabic.
items.note: Arabic is the language name used in the teaching tip and contrasted across countries in exercise 27.3.

learningObjectives: Name the continents and countries in the teaching-page geographical table, using capital letters for proper names.
Link country names to nationalities and recognise the common -(i)an, -ish and -ese endings and irregular forms.
Distinguish country names, nationality adjectives, people and language names, including Arabic as an important exception.
Match the ten capital cities in the exercises to their countries and use the capital of correctly.
Talk about languages spoken in different countries and explore the countries and geographical features in the exercises.

units.title: Unit 28 — Weather
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 28. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.note: Weather refers to conditions outdoors, such as sun, rain and wind. It is uncountable in this sense.

items.example: The sun is behind a cloud.
items.note: Sun is a noun. Sunny describes conditions, while shine is a verb used with the sun.

items.example: There is snow on the mountains.
items.note: Snow can be a noun or a verb. Snowy describes a condition; snowing describes an action.

items.example: We often get rain in April.
items.note: Rain is a noun and a verb; rainy is an adjective, and raining is the ongoing verb form.
A cloud is a visible mass in the sky. Cloudy is the corresponding weather adjective.

items.example: There is fog on the road.
items.note: Fog means low cloud that makes it difficult to see clearly. Foggy is the adjective.
Wind, meaning moving air, is pronounced /wɪnd/. The unrelated verb wind is usually pronounced /waɪnd/.

items.example: We heard thunder in the night.
items.note: Thunder is the sound that follows lightning; they often occur together in a thunderstorm.

items.example: We saw lightning before hearing thunder.
items.note: Lightning is a flash of electricity in a storm. Do not confuse the spelling with lightening.
Sunny is a weather adjective. Say It is sunny, not It is sunning.
Rainy is an adjective describing rainy conditions; it is raining describes an event happening now.

items.example: It is windy by the sea.
items.note: Windy is a weather adjective. It is windy is correct; it is winding has a different meaning.
Cloudy describes a sky with many clouds. Say it is cloudy, not it is clouding.

items.example: It is snowy in the mountains.
items.note: Snowy describes conditions with snow; it is snowing says snow is falling now.
Foggy describes low visibility caused by fog. It is foggy is the form taught in the book.
Thundery means likely to have or characterised by thunder and storms. Lightning has no matching common -y adjective.
It is raining is the present continuous. The textbook uses the contraction it’s raining.

items.example: It is snowing near the lake.
items.note: It is snowing means snow is falling at the moment; the textbook writes it’s snowing.

items.example: It rains a lot here in November.
items.note: It rains is a simple present description of habitual weather. The form is reinforced in exercise 28.3.

items.example: It snows in the mountains in winter.
items.note: It snows describes regular conditions; the exercise uses the structure When it snows, ...
Hot describes high temperature; use It is hot when talking about the weather.
Cold describes low temperature; compare warm for a less extreme, pleasantly mild condition.

items.example: It is warm and sunny today.
items.note: Warm means pleasantly or moderately hot; the source describes June as warm and sunny.

items.example: Spring is wet in this region.
items.note: Wet weather has a lot of rain; the book contrasts wet with dry.
Dry weather has little rain; the book uses the Sahara as an example.
A degree is a unit of temperature. Use degrees after numbers such as twenty or minus five.

items.example: It is minus three degrees outside.
items.note: Use minus before a temperature below zero, such as minus ten degrees.
An umbrella protects you from rain. The source uses carry an umbrella.

items.example: A hurricane can cause great damage.
items.note: A hurricane is a powerful tropical storm with very strong winds; it is not just any windy day.
A storm typically involves strong wind and rain in the book’s explanation.

items.example: There was a thunderstorm last night.
items.note: A thunderstorm includes thunder and lightning, often with rain and sometimes strong wind.

items.example: We went sightseeing on a dry day.
items.note: Sightseeing is visiting interesting places as a tourist. The book uses go sightseeing, with go.
Shine means give out light. The past form is shone (British English), illustrated in exercise 28.3.

items.example: The sun shone every morning last week.
items.note: Shone is a past form and past participle of shine, used for the sun in exercise 28.3.

items.example: The sun is shining over the hills.
items.note: The sun is shining describes sunlight now; the text uses the shorter expression the sun is shining.

items.example: What's the weather like in May?
items.note: What’s the weather like? asks about weather conditions, not personal likes or dislikes.

items.example: It's a sunny day in Bristol.
items.note: It’s a sunny day combines a + weather adjective + singular count noun day.

items.example: It's a lovely day for a walk.
items.note: It’s a lovely day is a positive comment about the weather.

items.example: It’s a horrible day to go cycling.
items.note: It’s a horrible day is a negative comment about the weather; horrible is stronger than bad.

items.example: I checked the weather forecast online.
items.note: A weather forecast tells you what the weather is expected to be like; the book suggests watching one in English.

items.example: June is usually warm and sunny here.
items.note: Usually describes what happens most of the time; use warm and sunny to describe typical weather.

items.example: It is often hot in summer.
items.note: Use in before seasons: in summer, in winter. This form occurs on the teaching page.

items.example: It is often cold in winter.
items.note: Use in before seasons: in winter. The phrase also occurs in exercise 28.4.

items.example: On a rainy day, I prefer reading.
items.note: A rainy day is a day with rain; this phrase appears in the free-response exercise.

items.example: We usually have sunny weather in July.
items.note: Sunny weather is an uncountable noun phrase: do not say a sunny weather.

items.example: We can go sightseeing when the weather is dry.
items.note: Go sightseeing is the collocation on the teaching page, and the textbook phonemic index lists this phrase.

items.example: It was minus five degrees this morning.
items.note: The book uses temperatures below zero to teach minus + number + degrees. The number five is an original pedagogical example.

items.example: It is cloudy in the city today.
items.note: Say it is cloudy to describe the sky; the textbook usually uses the contraction it’s.

learningObjectives: Identify the illustrated weather phenomena: sun, rain, snow, cloud, fog, wind, thunder and lightning.
Form and use weather adjectives such as sunny, cloudy, windy, foggy, snowy, rainy and thundery.
Distinguish weather conditions from ongoing actions: it is snowy versus it is snowing, and it is rainy versus it is raining.
Talk about temperature, wet and dry conditions, hurricanes, storms, thunderstorms and weather forecasts.
Ask what the weather is like, describe typical local weather and avoid the listed -ing-form errors.
